Class AbstractPanelElement<SELF extends AbstractPanelElement<SELF>>

java.lang.Object
com.trevorschoeny.menukit.core.AbstractPanelElement<SELF>
All Implemented Interfaces:
PanelElement
Direct Known Subclasses:
Button, Checkbox, Divider, Dropdown, DropdownMulti, Flow, Icon, InfoBox, ItemDisplay, ProgressBar, Radio, ScrollContainer, Slider, TextField, TextLabel, Toggle
public abstract class AbstractPanelElement<SELF extends AbstractPanelElement<SELF>> extends Object implements PanelElement
Abstract base for library-provided PanelElement implementations. Holds the cross-cutting state every concrete element needs (visibility — imperative + supplier-driven) so individual elements don't each re-implement the same pattern.

Why an abstract base, not just defaults on the interface

Java interfaces can't hold instance state (no fields), so a supplier-driven visibility flag has to live somewhere concrete. Two options were considered: (a) add the field + chainable showWhen() to every element class (Button, Toggle, Checkbox, etc. — ~14 classes, ~5 lines each), or (b) introduce this base and let library elements extend it. We took (b) because every library element implements PanelElement directly (no other supers to clash with) and the duplication-vs-base trade tips toward base when new cross-cutting chainables (.disabled() etc.) become free to add later in one place.

Consumer custom elements

The PanelElement interface stays as the consumer-facing extension point — custom elements can implement PanelElement directly and provide their own PanelElement.isVisible() override if they need conditional visibility. They lose the chainable .showWhen() sugar but the dispatch sites only consult isVisible() so functionality is identical.

Visibility precedence

Mirrors Panel.showWhen(BooleanSupplier): when showWhen(BooleanSupplier) is called with a non-null supplier, the supplier drives isVisible(). setVisible(boolean) silently no-ops while a supplier is active (consumer holds the state, library reads via supplier). Clearing with showWhen(null) reverts to imperative control and resets visible = true.

Self-type parameter (SELF) — fluent chaining without downcasts

The class is parameterized on its own concrete type (SELF extends AbstractPanelElement<SELF>). Every cross-cutting chainable setter here (showWhen, tooltip, at, setElementOpaque, declId, …) returns SELF via the abstract self() hook, which each concrete subclass implements as return this. This means a chain that starts with a Button stays typed as Button all the way through — no chain-order downcast trap, and per-widget covariant re-typing overrides (the old hand-written tooltip/showWhen narrowing overrides) are no longer needed. The curiously-recurring generic is purely a compile-time convenience: AbstractPanelElement is never referenced as a field/param/return type anywhere, only as a supertype, so the generic is fully contained to the class declarations.

      Element X within the panel content area. Mutable since §0047.

    • childY

      protected int childY
      Element Y within the panel content area. Mutable since §0047. This is the LIVE render Y — equal to the baseline plus any wrap-push the panel's reflow applied (see applyReflowedY(int)). Render, hit-test, and auto-size all read it (via the getter or, for consumer elements, the field directly), so it must always hold the live position.

    • self

      protected abstract SELF self()
      Returns this typed as the concrete subclass. Each subclass implements this as return this;. The base's chainable setters route their return through this hook so they hand back the concrete type instead of AbstractPanelElement, keeping fluent chains typed end-to-end.

    • isVisible

      public boolean isVisible()
      Returns whether this element is currently visible.

      If a visibility supplier is set (via showWhen(BooleanSupplier)), returns the supplier's current value. Otherwise returns the imperative visible field controlled via setVisible(boolean).

    • setVisible

      public void setVisible(boolean visible)
      Sets this element's imperative visibility.

      Silently no-ops when a showWhen(BooleanSupplier) supplier is active — the supplier owns visibility in that mode. Call showWhen(null) first to revert to imperative control.

    • showWhen

      public SELF showWhen(@Nullable BooleanSupplier supplier)
      Installs a supplier that drives this element's visibility. The supplier is consulted on every isVisible() call (typically every frame from render + every input dispatch), so keep it cheap.

      Mirrors Panel.showWhen(BooleanSupplier). The consumer-side mental model is "consumer holds the boolean source-of-truth; library reads via supplier"; same shape as Toggle.linked(int, int, int, int, BooleanSupplier, Consumer).

      Use case: 3 buttons in one panel, 2 conditionally visible. Without this you'd need two panels and a STACK_GAP between them.

      Pass null to clear the supplier and revert to imperative control. The prior setVisible(boolean) state is NOT restored — the element resets to default-visible (matching Panel.showWhen(BooleanSupplier)).

      Returns:
      this element, for method chaining.

    • setChildPosition

      public void setChildPosition(int x, int y)
      Moves this element's presentation position at runtime (§0047). Position is mutable presentation, not frozen structure — the element's identity, index, and sync participation are untouched. Client-side only.

      The render path (ctx.originX() + getChildX()) and the input path (PanelElement.hitTest(double, double, int, int), which composes contentX + getChildX()) both read position via the getters every frame, so the new position takes effect on the next frame. Panel auto-size (which walks getChildX()+getWidth()) likewise reflects it. Mirrors MKCSlot.setRenderPosition(x, y) on the slot side.

      Parameters:
      x - new panel-local X
      y - new panel-local Y

    • at

      public SELF at(int childX, int childY)
      Fluent positioning sugar — sets this element's panel-local position and returns the concrete element for chaining. Equivalent to setChildPosition(int, int) but chainable, so the simple widgets (Button, Toggle, Checkbox, Radio, Divider, ProgressBar, TextLabel, Icon, ItemDisplay) can be authored as new Button(...).at(x, y) instead of threading x/y through the constructor. Additive — the positional constructors still work; .at() just lets a consumer move the position out of the constructor argument list when that reads cleaner.
      Parameters:
      childX - panel-local X within the panel content area
      childY - panel-local Y within the panel content area
      Returns:
      this element, typed as the concrete subclass, for chaining

      The universal PanelElement tooltip contract — returns the .tooltip(...)-set supplier. Same backing field as the protected getTooltipSupplier() (which per-widget render code already reads); this public override exposes it through the interface so the shared PanelElement.queueTooltip(RenderContext) and any future uniform tooltip tooling can read it for every element type.

    • setElementOpaque

      public SELF setElementOpaque(boolean opaque)
      Sets whether this element is interaction-opaque (M9). When false, clicks/hover/tooltip over this element's bounds are NOT eaten by an opaque panel — they pass through to the slots or screen behind it (a "hole"). Default true (inherit the panel's opaque behavior).

      Input-layer only, matching M9's panel opacity (bounding-box, not visual alpha). Rendering is unaffected — a transparent hole that should also look empty simply has no element drawn over it.

      Returns:
      this element, for chaining

    • isElementOpaque

      public boolean isElementOpaque()
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Returns whether this element is interaction-opaque (M9 per-element opacity). When false, clicks/hover/tooltip over this element's bounds pass through an opaque panel to the slots/screen behind it (a click-through "hole"); when true (default) the element inherits the panel's opaque click-eating behavior.

      Input-layer only — mirrors M9's panel opacity (bounding-box, not visual alpha). The panel's click-consumption (ScreenPanelRegistry) consults this before eating a click that lands on this element's bounds.

      Specified by:

    • getElementDeclId

      public @Nullable String getElementDeclId()
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      The element's explicit, stable declaration id within its panel, or null to use the default identity (its registration position in the panel's element list).

      The panel-element identity contract (THE ONE WINDOW, Address keystone). Every addressable thing needs a deterministic, reopen-stable identity so the window can resolve it by address across a screen reopen (Minecraft rebuilds the menu and all elements each open). For a panel element that identity is, by default, its registration position in the panel's immutable, consumer-built element list — the same deterministic registration-order basis a created slot uses for its localIndex. Position-as-identity is stable as long as the consumer builds the element list in the same order each open (the normal case).

      This accessor is the explicit override for when list order is not a reliable identity (e.g. a consumer who conditionally includes some elements and wants a fixed handle regardless of order): supply a stable string and the window keys on it instead of position. Mirrors the consumer-supplied-string precedent a created slot has via its panel id.

      Default null (custom consumer elements implementing this interface directly inherit position-based identity). Library elements extending AbstractPanelElement can set an explicit id via declId(String).

      Specified by:
      getElementDeclId in interface PanelElement
